newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: The dreaded 'D' word haunts Philippine peso.
newsitem.headline: The dreaded 'D' word haunts Philippine peso.

text.p: The Philippine peso came under pressure on Monday after an article in a Sunday Singapore newspaper used the dreaded word "devaluation".

The newspaper quoted Philippine finance secretary Roberto de Ocampo as saying on Saturday that the peso could "devalue" against the U.S. dollar in coming weeks as Thailand's financial woes spill into the rest of the region.
But he was not quoted directly and the central bank was quick to knock down the article on Monday, saying De Ocampo was misquoted.
Nevertheless, the central bank was obliged to move in with aggressive intervention, selling dollars at 26.40, according to traders.
It also raised its one-day reverse repo rate to 30 percent from 24 percent to protect the peso. As a result, the peso managed to stand its ground.

But analysts said economic similarities with Thailand mean the Philippine currency is vulnerable to further attack and it remained to be seen how long the economy could realistically bear high interest rates.
"The peso is in trouble for a number of reasons -- mainly because the Philippines is at a similar stage economically as Thailand with the same structural problems," one analyst said.
This mainly manifests itself in the Philippine's need to attract foreign capital inflows to cover a current account deficit which is 4.0 to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product.
The Philippines only has around 30-35 percent of the foreign exchange reserves that Thailand has.
However, a speculative attack on the peso would be more difficult to mount given that the forward market is only accessible to resident firms for the purpose of hedging commercial transactions.
Central bank approval is required for all forward transactions.
So any selling has to be on the spot market and the best access to the peso comes from selling Philippine shares.

This together with high interest rates, a tough real exchange rate and a neighbouring country (Thailand) having a competitive currency means the pressure on the peso will start to build, analysts said.
In reaction to the newspaper article De Ocampo said, "The Philippine peso is based on market forces and not determined by the government."
The question is, is the peso actually floating?
It is this kind of statement that causes much head scratching in the market as the dollar/peso graph has looked like the heart monitor of a dead man for the past year and a half.
"When I look at my Reuters screen the peso has been 26.10 to 26.40 for a year and a half and that is not because demand and supply are balanced," said one trader.
"It's because they've fixed it and they are targeting it. Their reactions, if anything, make the situation more unstable given that fixed exchange rates are vulnerable to shocks."
The word devaluation itself is contentious. A devaluation can only come if a currency moves from one fixed rate to another, or from a fixed rate to a floating one.
The latter is what happened to sterling in 1992 as it was quasi-fixed in the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) but moved to a float after speculative attack.
If a currency is floating and it falls, it is not a devaluation, it is a depreciation.

"If De Ocampo keeps saying it's a flexible currency then he really shouldn't mention devaluation because that just sounds dramatic," said Angus Armstrong, chief economist Asia at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Singapore.
"Whether the Philippines has an objective of having a gradual depreciation over time is totally different. That is something which would not be too surprising."
